name: histogram
renderNote: The bands, their values, the edge ticks and the axis captions are one `<svg>`. A band is as wide as its range on the x axis and as tall as its value per unit of range, so its area is its value; bands of one width draw exactly as a gapless bar chart would.

projection.frame: each bar is one band of the range, and its area is that band's share

description: One quantity cut into bands that join end to end: each bar is as wide as its band and its area is the band's share, with an optional log axis for bands that widen toward the tail.
purpose: Use when the question is how a quantity is spread: annual losses, claim sizes, deal sizes, response times. Each row is a band (`$1M..$10M`) and its share or count. The x axis is a number line, so bands of different widths draw honestly, and `log` in the axis line keeps a long tail readable.

title.description: Slide heading — say what the shape shows ('Most years stay under $10M; one in thirty tops $100M'), not 'Loss histogram'.

axes.description: Optional axis line, as ONE bracketed list in its own paragraph ABOVE the heading: x first, then y — `[{Annual loss, $1M..$250M, log}, {Share of years}]`. The x member is `{name, min..max, log}`: the domain is optional and derives from the bands, and `log` draws a log scale, which needs every band edge above zero. The y member is only a name; a histogram prints its values on the bars, not on a value axis. The paragraph is consumed and painted on the axes. Same idiom as `scatter` and `quadrant`.

bands.description: One li per band, in order along the axis: a range pill and a value pill, in either order — `` `$1M..$10M` `55%` ``. `..` is the only range delimiter. Optional lead text names the band (`Attritional `$0..$5M` `61%``); without it the band is named by its range. Bands should join end to end: a gap draws as empty space and an overlap draws two bars over the same stretch, and `lint:deck` names both.

detail.description: Optional nested sublist under a band. It opens on hover or tap in Present, and folds into the speaker note in the PDF.

stressDoc.summary: Twelve equal bands on a linear axis, the tail bands under one percent.

whenToUse.title: The shape of a distribution
whenToUse.body: A histogram earns its slide when the question is how a quantity is spread: where most of it sits and how long the tail is. To compare separate categories, use `bar`; for the chance of exceeding each loss, use `ep-curve`.

whenToUse.title: Bands that widen toward the tail
whenToUse.body: Loss and claim bands usually widen ($1M, $10M, $50M, $250M). Write them as they are and add `log` to the axis line: each bar keeps its true area, and the tail stays readable.

antiPatterns.title: Categories that are not a number line
antiPatterns.body: Regions, products or lines of business are separate things, not bands of one quantity. Use `bar`, which leaves gaps between them.

antiPatterns.title: A dash for a range
antiPatterns.body: `$1M-$10M` is not a band: the dash reads two ways beside a negative number. Write `$1M..$10M`.

related.name: bar
related.when: separate categories compared by size, not bands of one quantity

related.name: ep-curve
related.when: the chance of a loss above each amount, read as a return period

commonMistakes.mistake: Expecting equal-height bars for equal shares when the bands differ in width.
commonMistakes.fix: A bar's AREA is its share, so a band five times as wide with the same share is a fifth as tall. That is what keeps a wide tail band honest; the value printed on the bar is the share.

dataShapeGuidance: Each row is a band `a..b`, with b above a, and a value. A row without both, or a band that does not climb (`$10M..$1M`), is left out.
A value below zero draws with no height, because an area cannot be negative; `lint:deck` warns. For signed values use `bar`.
`log` needs the whole axis above zero, the bands and any axis domain; otherwise the chart draws a linear axis, and `lint:deck` says so.

budget.note: Counted in BANDS. Editorial: past ten bands in a pane the value labels over narrow bands give way to the hover card.
